title: Faker heads into his third Asian Games with gold on his mind
summary: Faker heads into his third Asian Games with gold on his mind  Esports.gg
content:
Patrick covers competitive gaming and the business of esports for esports.gg. His work ranges from Dota 2, Counter-Strike 2, VALORANT, and fighting games to sponsorships, broadcast deals, viewership, team ownership, and…

South Korea's League of Legends legend heads to Aichi-Nagoya with gold in his sights and a roster of veteran analysts backing him up.

Lee 'Faker' Sang-hyeok is gearing up for his third consecutive Asian Games appearance. Is the gold medallist feeling the pressure? Not a chance. At a send-off ceremony held in Seoul, the League of Legends icon told attendees that the weight of public expectation, rather than hindering him, actually fires him.

"It is an honor and I am grateful to compete in the Asian Games for the third consecutive time," Faker said. "I feel a heavy sense of responsibility accordingly, and that feels more like great inspiration than pressure. I will approach this Asian Games with a sense of purpose, knowing that I am doing something meaningful."

Faker — so revered in his home country that he was appointedYouth Cyber Gambling Awareness ambassador in July— carried the South Korean flag at the Jakarta-Palembang Games in 2018, when esports debuted as a demonstration sport. He walked away with silver. Four years later in Hangzhou, when esports was an official medal event, Faker went one better, winning gold. It’s the kind of resume heading into a third consecutive appearance that other LoL players can only dream of.

Faker has also charmed the locals, reportedly spending time in the athletes' village taking photos and signing autographs for around 1,000 fellow competitors from other sports. The man is genuinely famous now — but fame doesn’t seem to be fazing him. He addressed the moment at the Seoul ceremony, saying with characteristic understatement: "I did take a lot of photos during the last tournament, but to be honest, it wasn't quite that many. Still, it was a deeply gratifying experience."

title: Has Fearless Draft actually improved champion diversity in League of Legends?
summary: Has Fearless Draft actually improved champion diversity in League of Legends?  Esports Insider
content:
Hajrudin Krdzic is a gaming and esports writer with over five years of experience covering live-service updates and competitive scenes. His first love was RTS games, which naturally grew into a long-term passion for MOBAs like League of Legends. He has also occasionally dipped into tactical shooters like Counter-Strike 2, roguelikes like Hades, and hero shooters such as Overwatch and Marvel Rivals.

Chadley Kemp (preferably just "Chad") has nearly a decade of editorial experience spanning esports, gaming, crypto, and betting content, covering everything from Counter-Strike and VALORANT to League of Legends and Dota 2. Outside of esports, Chadley holds a Ph.D. in Physiology and has published research in several peer-reviewed scientific journals.

TheLeague of Legendspro circuit used to have a drafting problem, but hasFearless Draftactually changed that?

In the past, you could finish game 1 of a best-of-five, load into game 2, and see half of the same champions again. Maybe they swapped sides or banned a priority pick, but more often than not, you are basically watching another version of the same draft.

Even at Worlds, things could get stale by the time we reached the knockout stage. Teams end up handshaking drafts, and suddenly, we’re watching the same boringCorkivs.Azirmatchup in mid lane over and over again. Fearless Draft was supposed to change that.

On paper, the format inevitably creates variety. If a best-of-five series reaches game 5, 40 champions have already been removed through the previous picks before the regular bans even begin. But that raises a more interesting question:
